obtaining IFR clearance from uncontrolle: Obtaining IFR Clearance from Uncontrolled Airports

overview: I3202 is the arrival-and-departure planning bridge between GPS procedures and instrument navigation. The event standard is to understand STAR clearances, identify Trouble T and ODP requirements, get an IFR clearance when no tower is available, and build an RNAV vector-to-final setup correctly.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: A STAR is an ATC-coded IFR arrival route that simplifies clearance delivery and transitions the aircraft from en route structure toward an instrument approach.

children.text: You must have the STAR chart available to accept the clearance.
RNAV STARs require an FMS-equipped aircraft and a current database procedure.
Mandatory crossing altitudes and speeds are binding when included in the clearance; "expect" altitudes and speeds are planning information until ATC assigns them.
MEAs are not STAR restrictions, but you must still remain above required en route minimum altitudes.
"Cleared the arrival" normally means fly the published lateral route and published speeds while maintaining the last assigned altitude until ATC authorizes descent.
"Descend via" authorizes lateral and vertical navigation on the arrival to comply with published altitude and speed restrictions, but not below the published bottom altitude.
When checking in on a new frequency while descending via, include the phrase "descending via" so the next controller knows your vertical clearance.
Do not use "expect" altitudes or speeds for lost-communication planning unless ATC specifically issued them as part of a further clearance.

items.text: The Trouble T symbol tells you non-standard takeoff minimums, obstacle information, or special departure procedures may apply.

children.text: The symbol appears on IAP, DP, ODP, or SID charts and points you to the takeoff minimums and obstacle-departure information for that airport.
The details are grouped by airport in the front section of the approach-plate or TPP booklet, usually alphabetically.
Trouble T is an obstacle-clearance alert; Navy takeoff weather minimums are related planning data but come from CNAF/OPNAV rules.
Read the actual text before departure. The symbol alone does not tell you the climb gradient, runway-specific restriction, or required route.
Some departures may still be legal with standard minimums if the aircraft meets a specific climb or routing requirement.
Convert any climb gradient in feet per NM into a required climb rate using groundspeed in NM per minute times the required feet per NM.

items.text: Obstacle Departure Procedures provide obstacle clearance from the terminal area to the en route structure when obstacles require something more specific than a diverse departure.

children.text: ODPs are labeled with "OBSTACLE" in the title on DoD/FAA charts.
They are developed when obstacles penetrate the departure obstacle-clearance surface and may be textual, graphical, or RNAV.
There is normally one ODP per runway, designed to provide the least restrictive obstacle-clearance route.
ODPs are not usually assigned by ATC unless needed for separation; the pilot must determine whether one exists and whether it should be flown.
Plan for higher-than-standard climb gradients, initial headings away from the intended course, special altitude restrictions, and close-in obstacles.
Check whether aircraft performance can meet the required gradient under expected conditions, including any emergency or degraded-performance plan.
If using an ODP, file or tell ATC clearly enough that the first controller understands the intended departure path.

items.text: Obtaining an IFR clearance from an uncontrolled airport is a preflight planning item, not a radio scramble at the hold-short line.

children.text: Common options include telephone clearance through FSS or ATC, published radio frequencies, RCO, UNICOM relay, direct ATC phone number, GCO, or a VFR departure to pick up IFR in the air when weather and rules allow.
A GCO is a remote ground-to-ground link used from the ground; four microphone clicks normally connects to ATC and six to AFSS when configured that way.
Plan the method before startup and have the backup method ready if the first contact path is saturated or unavailable.
If ATC issues a clearance void time, be airborne before the void time or contact ATC with intentions.
ATC also issues a notification time, no more than 30 minutes after the void time; failure to contact by that time can trigger overdue-aircraft action.
Once the void time passes, the IFR slot is released. Do not depart IFR on an expired clearance.
If departing VFR to pick up IFR, maintain VFR until the IFR clearance is received and accepted.

sections.title: Obtaining IFR Clearance from Uncontrolled Airports

items.text: RVFAC for RNAV approaches uses radar vectors to establish the aircraft on an RNAV final approach course while the FMS is configured for the correct leg and approach mode.

children.text: Load the RNAV approach from the current database with the correct runway and transition or vectors-to-final setup.
For a vector to final, build the final approach waypoint as the active leg, extend the intercept as required by the FMS, execute the modification, and set the PFD source to FMS.
Maintain ATC-assigned heading and altitude until established on the final approach course and cleared for the approach or otherwise cleared lower.
Keep the chart ahead of the FMS: the published procedure, not the magenta line alone, controls altitude, course, and missed-approach requirements.
Use RVFAC speed discipline from the radio-instrument pattern: 200 KIAS on downwind or extended final outside about 15 NM, and 150 KIAS on base unless directed otherwise.
Transition to before-approach configuration within 5 NM of the FAWP when established or being established on final.
Verify the HSI scale-change cue near 3 NM from the FAWP and APR annunciation near 2 NM from the FAWP.
If APR does not arm or GPS integrity is not available, use the authorized backup plan or continue at the appropriate altitude to the missed-approach point and execute the missed.

studyNotes.summary: Read arrivals and departures as clearances with consequences: know what ATC has authorized, what the chart requires, and how the FMS/RNAV setup supports the procedure.
